questions.ask: What does this container denote, and what are its key relations to nodes or links? Give an example.
Does this denote one managed router/system, or a more general topology node? Give a gloss, example, and key relations.
Does this denote a physical Ethernet port where one cable terminates, or a generic/logical termination point? State its scope and identity conditions.
Does this denote a logical bundled interface composed of physical member interfaces? Give an example and relations.
What are the source and target of this relation, and does it specifically express physical interfaces underlying a LAG?
Does this represent an actual physical connection, an LLDP-learned adjacency, or a more general logical topology link? Give endpoints and an example.
Is this nominal interface bandwidth in bits per second, measured traffic rate, or another rate? What entities can bear it?
Is this specifically the hardware/MAC address of a physical interface? Give its domain and example.
Does this denote an IPv4 address configured on an interface, and can its bearer be physical or logical?
Is this the routing identifier assigned to a node/device? Give an example and relations.
Is this the device-assigned interface name whose uniqueness is only node-local? Give an example.
What exactly is a tp-id: a device-local integer such as SNMP ifIndex, a topology-scoped opaque identifier, an interface name, or something else? State uniqueness scope and example.

answers.gloss: One managed topology: the container comprising the nodes and links managed together.
answers.relations: Contains/organizes b.node and b.link objects; b.node is explicitly part-of this network.

answers.gloss: A network device as represented in the topology; it is not restricted by the model to routers only.
answers.relations: Part-of b.network; bears b.rid and hosts b.tp and b.lag termination points.

answers.gloss: A non-LAG termination point on a node representing one physical port where a link can end. Its identity is the topology TP object/opaque TP identifier, not its interface name, MAC address, or ifIndex.
answers.relations: On b.node; can terminate b.link; can be a target of b.member; bears b.mac, b.ip, and b.ifname.

answers.gloss: A logical bundled termination point whose lag flag is true, combining multiple physical termination points on the same node so they act as one.
answers.example: tp-9d33f163 on node-0d30dd9a, composed over two physical member TPs
answers.relations: On b.node and has-member b.tp through b.member.

answers.gloss: The membership reference from a LAG termination point to each physical termination point underlying that bundle.
answers.relations: Source is b.lag; target is b.tp; specifically expresses physical-port membership in a LAG.

answers.gloss: An actual physical connection represented as a directed source-to-destination adjacency between termination points on different nodes; it is not merely LLDP remote-system descriptive data.
answers.relations: Has source and destination b.tp endpoints and bears b.rate.

answers.gloss: The nominal bandwidth of a link in kilobits per second, not a measured traffic rate.
answers.relations: Attribute of b.link, rather than directly of b.tp or b.node.

answers.gloss: The hardware/MAC address of a physical, non-LAG termination point.
answers.relations: Identifier of b.tp.

answers.gloss: An IP address held at layer 3 by a b.tp; in this model b.tp is the physical, non-LAG termination-point concept.
answers.relations: Address on b.tp.

answers.gloss: The routing identifier assigned to a topology node/device.
answers.relations: Identifier of b.node.

answers.gloss: The interface name supplied by the device for the interface represented by a termination point. It is understood in the context of that device/node rather than as a network-global identifier.
answers.example: et-0/0/1; a bundled interface may be named ae3
answers.relations: Identifier of b.tp.

answers.gloss: An opaque identifier for a termination-point object, not a device-local integer ifIndex and not the device-assigned interface name. The model does not state a stronger uniqueness scope, but examples function as topology object IDs.
answers.relations: Identifier of b.tp; it has no shared-reference binding.

questions.ask: Does this denote the managed network device/system itself or any node in a topology? Give its relations and shared reference binding, if any.
Is this specifically one physical port, or can it also be a logical interface such as a LAG? What identifies it, what can terminate on it, and what is its shared reference binding?
Is this a LAG/link-bundle interface composed of physical interfaces? Give its membership relations and shared reference binding.
What are the source and target of this relation? Does it specifically represent physical member interfaces underlying a LAG, or generic interface layering? Give its shared reference binding.
Does this denote LLDP remote-system observations, an actual physical cable/connection, or a topology adjacency inferred from discovery? State its endpoints, example, and shared reference binding.
Is this nominal interface speed or physical-link bandwidth, in what units, and which entity bears it? Give its shared reference binding.
Is this the hardware address of a physical interface, and can logical interfaces bear it? Give its shared reference binding.
Is this an IPv4 address configured on an interface, and may that interface be physical or logical? Give its shared reference binding.
What entity bears this routing identifier, and what is its shared reference binding?
Is this the device-assigned, device-local interface name for both physical and logical interfaces? Give its shared reference binding.
Is this specifically the device-local SNMP ifIndex integer, or some other interface identifier? State its uniqueness scope and shared reference binding.

answers.gloss: One managed router/system whose own interfaces and LLDP observations are reported, rather than an arbitrary topology container.
answers.relations: Hosts a.if and a.agg; bears a.rid. Shared reference: network-device.

answers.gloss: One physical Ethernet interface where exactly one cable ends; it excludes logical LAG interfaces. Its device-assigned name and integer index are only device-local identifiers.
answers.relations: On a.device; may have a.nbr, a.speed, a.mac, a.ip, a.ifname, and a.ifindex; may underlie a.agg through a.lower. Shared reference: physical-port.

answers.gloss: A logical LAG/link-bundle interface combining multiple physical interfaces of the same device so they act as one.
answers.example: ae3 on ywg-cr-00 over et-0/0/1 and et-0/0/2
answers.relations: On a.device; layered over member a.if interfaces through a.lower. Shared reference: link-bundle.

answers.gloss: The bundle-membership/layering relation from an aggregate interface to each physical interface underneath it; it is specifically used here for LAG membership.
answers.relations: Source is a.agg and target is a.if. Shared reference: bundle-membership.

answers.gloss: An LLDP-learned adjacency describing the far system and far port at the other end of a local physical interface's cable.
answers.example: et-0/0/1 on ywg-cr-00 sees et-0/0/2 on yxe-cr-03
answers.relations: Learned on local a.if; identifies the neighbouring system and port. Its representation is discovery data, although its bound reference is physical-connection.

answers.gloss: The nominal bandwidth of an interface, not measured traffic throughput, expressed in bits per second.
answers.relations: Attribute of a.if. Shared reference: nominal-speed.

answers.gloss: The layer-2 hardware/MAC address of a physical interface.
answers.relations: Identifier of a.if; the model does not assign this concept to a.agg. Shared reference: hardware-address.

answers.gloss: An IPv4 address configured on an interface; the concept can apply to a logical aggregate interface as illustrated by ae3, as well as to an interface generally.
answers.relations: Address on an interface. Shared reference: ip-address.

answers.gloss: The routing identifier of a managed device.
answers.relations: Identifier of a.device. Shared reference: router-id.

answers.gloss: The interface name assigned by the device, unique only within that device; it covers physical names such as et-0/0/1 and logical aggregate names such as ae3.
answers.relations: Identifier of an interface in the context of its a.device. Shared reference: interface-name.

answers.gloss: An arbitrary device-local integer interface index, specifically the SNMP-style ifIndex rather than an opaque topology object ID.
answers.relations: Identifier of an interface, unique only within its a.device. Shared reference: interface-index.

answers.gloss: A network device as represented as a node in the managed topology. Exact shared-reference entry: network-device.
answers.relations: Part of b.network; hosts termination points and bears b.rid.

answers.gloss: A non-LAG physical termination point representing one physical port. Exact shared-reference entry: physical-port.
answers.relations: On b.node; terminates b.link; may be a member of b.lag and bear MAC, IP, and interface-name data.

answers.gloss: A logical bundled termination point combining physical member termination points. Exact shared-reference entry: link-bundle.
answers.example: tp-9d33f163 over two physical member TPs
answers.relations: On b.node; has b.tp members through b.member.

answers.gloss: The relation from a LAG termination point to each physical termination point belonging to it. Exact shared-reference entry: bundle-membership.
answers.relations: From b.lag to b.tp.

answers.gloss: A represented physical connection between termination points on different nodes. Exact shared-reference entry: physical-connection.
answers.relations: Has source and destination b.tp endpoints and bears b.rate.

answers.gloss: Nominal link bandwidth in kilobits per second. Exact shared-reference entry: nominal-speed.
answers.relations: Attribute of b.link.

answers.gloss: The hardware/MAC address of a physical termination point. Exact shared-reference entry: hardware-address.
answers.relations: Identifier of b.tp.

answers.gloss: An IP address held by a termination point at layer 3. Exact shared-reference entry: ip-address.
answers.relations: Address on b.tp.

answers.gloss: The routing identifier of a topology node/device. Exact shared-reference entry: router-id.
answers.relations: Identifier of b.node.

answers.gloss: The device-assigned name of the interface represented by a termination point. Exact shared-reference entry: interface-name.
answers.relations: Identifier of a termination point/interface in its node context.

proposals.rationale: Both are bound to the same shared reference, network-device.
Both are bound to physical-port and denote a non-LAG physical interface where a cable/link terminates.
Both are bound to link-bundle and denote a logical LAG composed of physical interfaces.
Both are bound to bundle-membership and relate a LAG to each underlying physical interface.
Both are bound to physical-connection. Although A represents it as LLDP-learned remote-system data and B as a topology link, the identical shared reference settles the correspondence.
Both are bound to nominal-speed and denote nominal bandwidth rather than measured traffic rate; their units and immediate modeled bearer differ.
Both are bound to hardware-address and identify a physical interface.
Both are bound to ip-address. A explicitly permits aggregate bearers while B attaches it to b.tp, but the common reference settles the concept correspondence.
Both are bound to router-id and identify the managed node/device for routing.
Both are bound to interface-name and denote the device-assigned, device-contextual interface name.
Both are bound to the shared reference network-device and denote the managed network device represented as a node.
Both are bound to physical-port and denote a non-LAG physical interface where a cable or physical link terminates.
Both are bound to link-bundle and denote a logical aggregate/LAG composed of physical member interfaces.
Both are bound to bundle-membership and relate a LAG to its underlying physical member interfaces.
Both are bound to physical-connection, which settles correspondence despite A encoding LLDP-learned far-end data and B encoding a topology link.
Both are bound to nominal-speed and denote nominal bandwidth rather than measured traffic rate; units and immediate modeled bearer differ.
Both are bound to hardware-address and denote the MAC address of a physical interface.
Both are bound to ip-address. Their modeled bearer coverage differs, but the common shared reference settles correspondence.
Both are bound to router-id and denote the routing identifier of a managed device/node.
Both are bound to interface-name and denote a device-assigned interface name interpreted in device/node context.

The concepts share reference physical-port and both exclude LAG interfaces.
The concepts share reference link-bundle and denote the same logical bundled interface.
The concepts share reference bundle-membership and have matching LAG-to-physical-port direction.
The shared reference physical-connection settles the correspondence despite representational differences.
The shared reference nominal-speed settles the correspondence; both denote nominal bandwidth.
The concepts share reference hardware-address and identify physical interfaces.
The shared reference ip-address settles correspondence despite differences in modeled bearer coverage.
The concepts share reference router-id and have the same meaning.
The concepts share reference interface-name and denote the same device-contextual name.
Both concepts are bound to network-device and denote the same managed network device represented in the topology.
Both are bound to physical-port and denote a non-LAG physical interface or termination point where a physical connection ends.
Both are bound to link-bundle and denote a logical LAG composed of physical member interfaces.
Both are bound to bundle-membership and express the relation from a LAG to its underlying physical interfaces.
Both are bound to physical-connection, which settles correspondence despite their different representations of the connection.
Both are bound to nominal-speed and denote nominal bandwidth rather than measured traffic throughput.
Both are bound to hardware-address and denote the MAC address of a physical interface.
Both are bound to ip-address; the shared reference settles correspondence despite differing modeled bearer coverage.
Both are bound to router-id and denote the routing identifier of the managed device or node.
Both are bound to interface-name and denote the device-assigned interface name interpreted in device context.
